# Geo-Filtered Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search on a Single Proximity Graph ### Abstract Geo-filtered approximate nearest-neighbor (GFANN) search retrieves the objects inside a query-specified geographic disk whose feature vectors are closest to a query vector, a core operation in location-aware Web search. A disk filter on a standard proximity graph invalidates out-of-disk routing vertices; on selective disks, these removals break greedy paths and recall drops sharply. Existing methods scan all in-disk objects, over-fetch unfiltered candidates, or maintain separate sub-indexes across spatial partitions, trading latency for index overhead. We propose REACH, a single-graph index based on _row-local active-order invariance_: if every vertex stores its outgoing neighbors in a fixed-width row sorted by vector distance, any disk filter masks out-of-disk entries while surviving in-disk (_active_) neighbors remain vector-sorted. Offline, each vertex merges globally closest vector candidates with a nearest-first geographic stream into one row; online, beam search evaluates vector distances only for the first \(\ell\) active entries of each visited row. Because collected objects share the same distance to every query center, every disk admits a coordinate group in full or not at all, decomposing active connectivity into intra-group and inter-coordinate conditions. Under a spatial marked-site model with repeated coordinates, we prove that polylogarithmic out-degree guarantees strong connectivity across all disks and constant-factor distance reduction per hop on compact disks, while a cut-rank threshold characterizes the minimum scan budget \(\ell\). Across four datasets up to 107 objects, one REACH index per dataset outperforms SOTA methods, achieving 2.49\(\times\) higher geometric-mean QPS than the strongest baseline at 0.95 Recall@10 on selective queries, while building 3.8\(\times\)-11.9\(\times\) faster and using 37%-45% less space than a SOTA spatial-graph index. ### CCS Concepts • **Information systems** \(\rightarrow\) **Retrieval models and ranking: Spatial-temporal systems.** ### Keywords Approximate nearest neighbor search, geo-filtered vector search, proximity graph index, spatial-vector retrieval ### 1 Introduction Approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search in high-dimensional vector spaces is a core operation in Web search, recommendation, and retrieval-augmented generation [20, 27]. Proximity graphs such as HNSW [25], NSG [13], and DiskANN [17] achieve the strongest trade-off between recall and latency [41] by linking each object to proximate vector neighbors and routing queries through best-first beam search. In location-aware Web services, vector similarity is often paired with a spatial range filter: a user may search for geo- tagged photos visually similar to a query image within a kilometer of a landmark, or retrieve points of interest (POIs) matching a text query within walking distance. We call this problem _geo-filtered approximate nearest-neighbor_ (GFANN) search: given a query vector and a query-centered geographic disk, return the _k_ in-disk objects closest to the query in vector space. Applying a geographic disk filter to a standard proximity graph breaks its navigation structure. Because semantic similarity is independent of physical location, a vertex’s closest vector neighbors are scattered globally; restricting traversal to a disk removes out-of-disk routing vertices, which severs multi-hop paths and disconnects the in-disk subgraph (_filter-induced path erosion_, Section 2). Existing filtered ANN methods struggle as disk selectivity varies [8]. Filter-agnostic strategies fail at one extreme: (1) _pre- filtering_ (_Spatial-First_ [7]) scans all in-disk objects, which is fast on tiny radii but slows by orders of magnitude on neighborhood- or city-scale disks (102-106 objects); (2) _post-filtering_ (_Vector-First_, VBASE [46]) retrieves global vector candidates before spatial filtering, wasting most distance evaluations on selective disks; and (3) _in-filtering_ (ACORN [28]) explores two-hop unfiltered neighborhoods, which still disconnect under selective disks. Predicate-aware indexes encode filters into the graph for discrete labels [6, 15, 24, 42], workload-tuned sub-indexes [21], weighted attribute–vector metrics [40, 45], or 1D numeric intervals [12, 23, 43, 47, 48]. However, 1D range graphs rely on a global attribute order under which every interval is contiguous; 2D disks admit no such order even on three objects and induce \(\Omega(n^2)\) distinct active sets (Section 2), whereas spatial partitions [37, 44] either split queries across cell graphs or duplicate edges across tree levels. In this paper, we show that a _single_ static graph of fixed out- degree can support arbitrary geographic disks through _Ranked Active-Graph Recovery_. Under any disk _c_, out-of-disk entries in row(_u_) are ignored while surviving in-disk (_active_) entries remain sorted by vector distance. Retaining all active entries defines the complete active projection \(\mathcal{H}_\infty(c)\), which sets the recall ceiling on _c_; scanning row(_u_) sequentially and taking only the first \(\ell\) active entries reconstructs a degree-\(\ell\) _recovery graph_ \(\mathcal{H}_\ell(c)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_\infty(c)\) that caps per-step vector evaluations at \(\ell\), with minimum connectivity budget given by the _cut-rank threshold_ \(\ell_\mathrm{SC}(c)\).

To keep \(\mathcal{H}_\infty(c)\) connected across all \(\Omega(n^2)\) disks on both POI catalogs with mostly unique coordinates and photo archives where thousands of records share a landmark coordinate \[1\], we group co-located objects into _coordinate fibers_. If a vertex simply linked to its geographically closest objects, a dense landmark would consume its entire neighbor budget on co-located ties. Because all members of a fiber lie at the same distance from any query center, any disk admits a fiber _either in full or not at all_. This property decomposes active connectivity into query-independent _intra-fiber connectivity_ and _inter-coordinate quotient connectivity_, both satisfied at polylogarithmic degree under a marked-site model. Guided by this analysis, REACH builds one width-_B_ row per vertex offline from global vector candidates and a fiber-aware geographic stream, and answers queries online through an _O(n_) spatial seed grid and a two-phase _filter-then-score_ kernel. Our contributions are:

\(\bullet\) **Theoretical Foundation:** We prove that 2D disks induce \(\Omega(n^2)\) active sets (Theorem 2.2) and admit no contiguous order (Proposition 2.3). We then define \(\mathcal{H}_\ell(c)\) and cut rank \(\ell_\mathrm{SC}(c)\) (Theorem 3.3), prove fiber closure and route decomposition (Lemma 3.4, Theorem 3.5), and establish polylogarithmic degree bounds for strong connectivity and compact-disk \(\alpha\)-shortcut routing (Theorem 3.7, Corollary 3.8).<tbc>

\(\bullet\) **Graph Index and Query Algorithms:** We develop REACH’s dual-source row assembly (Algorithm 1), which combines global vector candidates with a 3D kd-tree geographic stream, bounds coordinate ties through intra-fiber \(\alpha\)-pruning, and reuses vector<tbc>

\(\bullet\) **Comprehensive Evaluation:** Across four datasets up to 10<sup>7</sup> objects and six selectivities (\(\bar{\sigma}\in[10^{-5},1]\)), one REACH index per dataset achieves 2.49\(\times\) higher geometric-mean QPS than the best per-setting baseline at 0.95 Recall@10 on selective queries (fastest in 14/16 selective cells, 6.33\(\times\) over CubeGraph, 3.56\(\times\) over Geo-Partition), builds 3.8\(\times\)-11.9\(\times\) faster than CubeGraph, and uses 37%-45% less space on three of the four datasets.

## 2 Preliminaries

**Data Model and GFANN Queries.** Let \(\mathcal{D}=\{o_v=(x_v,s_v):v\in V\}\) be a dataset of _n_=|_V_| objects with identifiers _V_={1_,...,n_}. Each object \(v\in V\) has a feature vector \(x_v\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^D\) measured by Euclidean distance \(d(x,y)=\|x-y\|_2\) and a geographic coordinate \(s_v=(\lambda_v,\phi_v)\in\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathbb{S}^2\) measured by great-circle distance \(\Delta(s,t)\) (notation in Appendix B.1). A spatial filter _c_=(_g,r_) with center \(g\in\mathcal{S}\) and radius _r\>_0 defines the closed disk \(\Omega_c=\{s\in\mathcal{S}:\Delta(s,g)\le r\}\) and the _active set_ \(\mathcal{A}(c)=\{v\in V:\Delta(s_v,g)\le r\}\) of size _m_=|A(_c_)| and selectivity \(\sigma(c)=m/n\). Given a GFANN query _q_=(_x<sub>q</sub>,c<sub>q</sub>,k_) with _k<sub>q</sub>_=min{_k,m_}, the exact answer \(T_k(q)\subseteq\mathcal{A}(c_q)\) consists of the _k<sub>q</sub>_ active objects closest to _x<sub>q</sub>_ under \(v\prec_qw\Longleftrightarrow(d(x_q,x_v),v)\prec_\mathrm{lex}(d(x_q,x_w),w)\).

**Proximity Graphs, Beam Search, and Path Erosion.** To avoid scanning all _m_ active vectors in _O(mD_) time, ANN systems build a directed proximity graph _G_=(_V,E_) offline \[13, 17, 25\]: each vertex _u_ collects vector-proximate candidates and applies \(\alpha\)-witness diversification (discarding _w_ if an earlier neighbor _v_ satisfies \(\alpha d(x_v,x_w)\le d(x_u,x_w)\)) to cap out-degree at _B_ \[41\], forming _u_’s _row_ row(_u_). At query time, best-first _beam search_ maintains a pool of at most _L_ candidates ordered by \(d(x_q,\cdot)\) and expands the closest unvisited vertex until no pool candidate is closer than the _k_-th best result (Recall\(@k=|R\cap T_k(q)|/k_q\)). **Why 1D Range and Per-Condition Indexes Fail.** Range-filtered graphs \[12, 23, 43, 47, 48\] sort all objects into one global sequence \(a_1\le\cdots\le a_n\) so that every query interval is contiguous. Two geometric properties rule out this strategy for 2D disks (proof of Theorem 2.2 in Appendix A.3):

Theorem 2.2 (Disk Range Complexity). _The family_ \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D})=\{\mathcal{A}(c):c=(g,r),g\in\mathbb{S}^2,r\ge 0\}\) _of distinct disk active sets satisfies_ \(|\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D})|\le\sum_{i=0}^4\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{i}=O(n^4)\)_, and reaches_ \(|\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D})|=\Omega(n^2)\) _on worst-case n-object collections._

Proposition 2.3 (Absence of a Universal Contiguous Order). _Place three objects V_={1,2,3} _at the vertices of a small equilateral spherical triangle on_ S<sup>2</sup>_. A disk centered at the midpoint of any pair_ {_i,j_} _with radius_ \(\Delta(s_i,s_j)/2\) _admits only_ {_i,j}; because the first and last elements in any permutation of V are non-contiguous, no linear order makes_ A(_c_) _contiguous for all disks c._

## 3 Ranked Active-Graph Recovery Theory

Because 2D disks induce \(\Omega(n^2)\) active sets and admit no contiguous order, we serve all disks from a _single_ static graph _G=(V,E_) of bounded degree _B_ (complete proofs appear in Appendix A).

### 3.1 Active-Order Invariance and Recovery Graph

**Active-Order Invariance.** Our first observation is that _filtering a vector-sorted neighbor row preserves the relative vector-distance order of the surviving entries._ Suppose vertex _u_ stores its outgoing neighbors in a row row(_u_)=(_v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>B</sub>_) ordered strictly by distance _d(x<sub>u</sub>,x<sub>v</sub>_) (with ties broken by ID _v_, denoted \(v\prec_uw\)). Under disk _c=(g,r_), masking out-of-disk entries leaves the active subsequence \(C_u(c)=\mathrm{row}(u)\cap\mathcal{A}(c)=(v_i\in\mathrm{row}(u):v_i\in\mathcal{A}(c))\), which remains strictly sorted under \(\prec_u\). Let \(\mathrm{rank}_{u,c}(v)\in\{1,\dots,|C_u(c)|\}\) denote the 1-based ordinal rank of \(v\in C_u(c)\) within _C<sub>u</sub>(c_).

_Example 3.1._ Suppose row(_u_)=\[_a,b,c,d,e,f_\] is sorted by \(d(x_u,\cdot)\). Under disk _c<sub>q</sub>_, if {_a,c,d,e_} are active and {_b,f_} are inactive (Figure 4), filtering leaves _C<sub>u</sub>(c<sub>q</sub>_)=\[_a,c,d,e_\] with active ranks 1,2,3,4. For budget \(\ell=3\), a left-to-right scan skips _b_ and stops at the third active entry _d_ without reading _e_ or _f_, recovering \[_a,c,d_\].<tbc>

<tbc>_Definition 3.2 (Complete Active Projection and Recovery Graph)._ Given vector-sorted rows \(\{\mathrm{row}(u)\}_{u\in V}\), disk _c_, and integer _recovery budget_ \(\ell\ge 1\), the _recovery graph_ \(\mathcal{H}_\ell(c)=(\mathcal{A}(c),\{(u,v):u\in\mathcal{A}(c),v\in C_u(c),\mathrm{rank}_{u,c}(v)\le\ell\})\) retains the first \(\ell\) active row entries at each \(u\in\mathcal{A}(c)\), and \(\mathcal{H}_\infty(c)=G[\mathcal{A}(c)]\) is the _complete active projection._

Theorem 3.3 (Subgraph Monotonicity and Cut-Rank Threshold). _For any graph G=(V,E_) _of row width B, disk c, and budget_ \(\ell\ge 1\):_(a)_ \(\mathcal{H}_\ell(c)\) _is a spanning subgraph of_ \(\mathcal{H}_\infty(c)\) _with out-degree at most_ \(\mathrm{min}\{\ell,B\}\)_; (b)_ \(\mathcal{H}_\ell(c)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\ell^\prime}(c)\) _for_ \(\ell\le\ell'\) _and_ \(\mathcal{H}_B(c)=\mathcal{H}_\infty(c)\)_; and (c) for_ \(|\mathcal{A}(c)|\ge 2\), \(\mathcal{H}_\ell(c)\) _is strongly connected if and only if_ \(\ell\ge\ell_\mathrm{SC}(c)\)_, where the_ cut rank _is_

\(\ell_\mathrm{SC}(c)=\mathrm{max}_{\varnothing\neq S\subseteq\mathcal{A}(c)}\mathrm{min}_{u\in S,v\in C_u(c)\backslash S}\mathrm{rank}_{u,c}(v)\) (1)

_(with inner minimum_ \(\infty\) _if no edge of_ \(\mathcal{H}_\infty(c)\) _leaves S). In_ (1)_, any subset_ \(S\subseteq\mathcal{A}(c)\) _represents a potential isolated component: the inner minimum is the earliest active rank at which some vertex_ \(u\in S\) _has an edge leaving S, and the outer maximum is the worst-case cut across_ A(_c_) _(proof in Appendix A.1)._

### 3.2 Coordinate Fibers and Route Decomposition

**Coordinate Fibers and Closure.** Real geotagged datasets differ widely in coordinate multiplicity. In POI catalogs (Overture-1M), almost all records have distinct coordinates (_M≈n_); in social- media archives (Yfcc-Clip), 64.6% of coordinates are duplicates and up to 5,726 photos share a single landmark location \[1\]. To model the entire range \(1\le M\le n\), we group all objects at each distinct coordinate \(z\in\mathcal{S}\) into a _coordinate fiber_ \(F(z)=\{v\in V:s_v=z\}\).

## 3.3 Polylogarithmic Guarantees

**Coordinate Tie-Breaking and Two-Scale Selection.** To maintain connectivity on small disks, each vertex _u_ allocates a quota of _B<sub>g</sub>_ edges to geographically nearby candidates. If _u_ simply linked to its _B<sub>g</sub>_ geographically closest objects, a nearby landmark _z_ with thousands of co-located photos would fill all _B<sub>g</sub>_ slots with ties at _z_ and leave no edges to surrounding sites, violating Condition (ii) of<tbc>

<tbc>Theorem 3.5; conversely, keeping only one arbitrary object per site would disconnect multi-object fibers and violate Condition (i).

To satisfy both conditions, we model D by a regular marked point process \[9, 31\] (Appendix A.4): _M_ distinct sites _Z_<sub>1</sub>_,...,Z<sub>M</sub>_ are drawn on a compact, connected region \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathbb{S}^2\) with bounded density \(0<p_{s,-}\le p_s(z)\le p_{s,+}\), and each site _Z<sub>i</sub>_ hosts a fiber _F(Z<sub>i</sub>_) of size \(f_i\ge 1\) (\(\sum_{i=1}^Mf_i=n\)) whose vectors \(X_v\sim v_{Z_i,\Theta_i}\) come from a geodesic support of intrinsic dimension _d_<sub>X</sub>_\>_0, diameter _D<sub>x</sub>_, and doubling constant _C<sub>D</sub>_. Each vertex _u_ selects geographic edges using two rules: (1) _Intra-fiber_ \(\alpha\)_-witness rule_: within _F(z_), _u_ scans up to _K<sub>f</sub>_ candidates \(v\in F(z)\backslash\{u\}\) in ascending _d(x<sub>u</sub>,x<sub>v</sub>_) and retains _v_ unless an earlier retained \(w\in F(z)\) satisfies \(d(x_v,x_w)\le d(x_u,x_v)/\alpha\) (\(\alpha>1\)). (2) _Nearest-first coordinate stream: u_ visits sites \(z\neq s_u\) in nondecreasing \(\Delta(s_u,z)\) and applies Rule (1) inside each _F(z_) until _B<sub>g</sub>_ new edges are selected, with cumulative charge \(L_u(\rho)=\sum_{z:\Delta(s_u,z)\le\rho}\chi_u(z)\) within radius \(\rho\).

**Bounding Per-Site Quota Consumption.** Partition X\\{_x<sub>u</sub>_} into dyadic shells \[2<sup>-_k_</sup>_D_<sub>x</sub>,2<sup>-(_k_-1)</sup>_D_<sub>x</sub>\] from minimum separation \(\varepsilon_\alpha=\Theta((\delta/n^2)^{1/d_\mathcal{X}})\) to _D<sub>x</sub>_. Because any two \(\alpha\)-pruned survivors in the same shell are separated by \(>1/(2\alpha)\) of the shell radius, doubling packing limits each shell to \(\le P_\alpha=C_D^{\lceil log_2(4\alpha)\rceil}=O(1)\) survivors; across all shells, with probability \(\ge 1-\delta/3\)_, any site z of arbitrary size f<sub>z</sub> consumes at most_

\(a_\alpha=min\big\{K_f,P_\alpha\big(1+\big\lceil log_2(D_x/\varepsilon_\alpha)\big\rceil\big)\big\}=O\big(log(nM/\delta)\big)\) (2)

slots of _B<sub>g</sub>_. Meanwhile, RGG theory \[30, 31\] shows that linking active sites within radius \(\rho_c=C_s\sqrt{\lambda_2(\Omega_c)log(3M/\delta)/(M\pi_c)}\) (\(\pi_c=\int_{\Omega_c}p_sd\lambda_2\)) connects the coordinate quotient across \(\Omega_c\), with at most \(h_c=\lceil C_hlog(3M/\delta)\rceil\) sites per \(\rho_c\)-ball (Appendix A.5).

## 4 The Proposed REACH Index

To realize the guarantees of Section 3 in a single fixed-width graph, REACH stores one row row(_u_) of width _B=B<sub>v</sub>+B<sub>g</sub>_ for each vertex \(u\in V\) . Each row combines a _global-vector source_ of quota _B<sub>v</sub>_ (which provides long-range vector shortcuts on broad disks where \(\rho_c<\mathrm{diam}(\Omega_c)\)) with a _fiber-aware geographic stream_ of quota _B<sub>g</sub>_ (which provides local connectivity on selective disks under Theorem 3.7), and sorts all retained neighbors by \(d(x_u,\cdot)\).

## 6 Related Work

**Filtered and Hybrid ANN Search.** Proximity graphs searched with beam search (HNSW \[25\], NSG \[13\], DiskANN \[17\]) lead unfiltered ANN \[2, 3, 27, 41\]. For attribute filters \[8\], Filtered- DiskANN \[15\], UNG \[6\], and JAG \[42\] embed discrete labels into edges; CGIF \[24\] pairs HNSW with inverted files; SIEVE \[21\] builds workload-tuned sub-indexes; VBASE \[46\] uses relaxed monotonicity; NHQ \[40\] and DEG \[45\] define composite attribute-vector metrics; and ACORN \[28\] filters two-hop neighborhoods. However, 2D disks cannot be indexed by finite inverted lists and act as hard boundaries (\(\Delta(s_v,g_q)\le r_q\)). Range graphs (SeRF \[48\], uRNG \[23\], RNSG \[47\], WinFilter \[12\], iRangeGraph \[43\], UNIFY \[22\], DSG \[29\], DIGRA \[19\]) rely on a 1D attribute order absent for 2D disks.

**Spatial-Vector and Fiber-Navigable Retrieval.** Spatial \[14, 16, 34\] and geo-textual indexes \[7\] prune 2D space before secondary filtering (_Spatial-First, Geo-Partition_); REACH uses a flat grid only for \(\tau\) entry seeds. Mesh \[37\] tunes cell graphs for a known workload and switches between spatial scan and cell-graph search by selectivity, whereas CubeGraph \[44\] builds graphs across tree levels. Unlike FNS \[10\], which calls any predicate-induced subgraph a "fiber," our _coordinate fibers F(z_) are co-located object classes admitted in full or not at all by any disk (Lemma 3.4), which connects intra-fiber \(\alpha\)-pruning with RGG theory \[4, 9, 30-32\].

## 7 Conclusion

We proposed REACH for GFANN search via _Ranked Active-Graph Recovery_: (1) filtering a vector-sorted row preserves survivor order, recovering \(\mathcal{H}_\ell(c)\) governed by cut rank \(\ell_\mathrm{SC}(c)\); and (2) coordinate fibers pass or fail any disk filter as a unit, yielding polylogarithmic- degree connectivity and \(2.49\times\) higher selective QPS.

### B.1 Summary of Notation and System Overview

2 summarizes the notation used throughout the paper, and Figure 9 illustrates the six-module offline and online workflow of REACH. Offline construction produces two persistent data structures: the 4_nB_-byte table of vector-sorted rows and the _O(n_) spatial grid seed directory. Online, the query disk _c<sub>q</sub>_ defines the activity predicate evaluated during sequential row scanning, while the grid directory supplies \(\tau\) initial active seeds inside A(_c<sub>q</sub>_).

### B.2 Grid Directory and Entry Seeding

Algorithm 3 presents the spatial entry seeding procedure. The grid directory partitions latitude \([-90^\circ,90^\circ]\) and longitude \((-180^\circ,180^\circ]\) into cells of resolution \(w_\phi=w_\lambda=0.5^\circ\) (\(360\times 720=259,200\) cells)<tbc>

<tbc>and stores vertex identifiers in a contiguous array indexed by a prefix-sum offset table \[14, 34\]. Construction requires two linear counting passes (_\<_0.6 s at _n_=10<sup>7</sup>). At query time, Algorithm 3 expands Chebyshev rings \(\rho=0,1,\dots\) around the cell containing _g<sub>q</sub>_, where \(\text{mindist}(\kappa,g_q)\) is the exact minimum great-circle distance from _g<sub>q</sub>_ to cell \(\kappa\), halting once \(\tau=16\) active seeds are collected or \(min_{\kappa\in\mathcal{K}_\rho}\text{mindist}(\kappa,g_q)>r_q\). The zero-auxiliary-storage seeding alternative evaluated in Exp-5 replaces the grid directory with _N<sub>a</sub>_=256 anchor vertices selected via farthest-point sampling on the 3D unit sphere and descends the physical REACH graph using \(\Delta(\cdot,g_q)\) until \(\tau=16\) active vertices inside \(\Omega_{c_q}\) are reached.
